Content covers: the practical reason for using a single blood-basin stand rather than two (to prevent the Kohen Gadol from confusing the bull's and goat's blood); the thirteen shofar-boxes in the Temple and their labeled purposes (new shekels, old shekels, bird-offerings, burnt-offering birds, wood, frankincense, gold for the kapporet, and six for voluntary offerings); the detailed mechanics of each box (how the new-shekel and old-shekel funds are used, including the old-shekel surplus funding the city walls); R. Yehuda's own view that the voluntary-offering boxes fund the altar's supplementary offerings via the six ancestral priestly houses, cross-referenced to the end of Menachot; the resulting proof that R. Yehuda does, after all, accept written labels as reliable (creating the apparent tension the Gemara opened with); and the transition into the sugya about invalidating bird-offering coins when an owner has died, including the four-zuz valuation of a single bird and R. Yehuda's rejection of retroactive designation (bereirah), continuing into the Samaritan-wine terumah case.
